Alright, the latest attempt to benchmark the model with `m.compile(dynamic=True)` still crashes. The traceback indicates a dtype handling issue inside the Inductor backend when using dynamic compilation together with `torch.autocast` in the backward pass. The error didn’t appear when I ran the unit tests after swapping the custom STE for the detach‑based formulation, so the core model code is now compile‑friendly; it’s just this particular combination of dynamic compilation and autocast that’s problematic.

Given that, the most straightforward way to verify whether the model can be compiled at all is to drop the `dynamic=True` flag and let TorchDynamo/Inductor use its default (static) compilation mode. Static mode should avoid the dynamic shape handling that seems to trigger the dtype bug, while still giving me a compiled graph for the forward pass. If that works, I’ll at least have a baseline performance figure and can later investigate dynamic support separately.

I’ll reuse the same benchmarking script I used earlier for the dynamic case, because it already captures both a warm‑up compile phase (running a few loops with increasing depth) and a steady‑state throughput measurement (20 random steps). The only change needed is to call `m.compile()` with no arguments. I’ll keep the autocast context (bf16) because that’s the intended inference precision, and I’ll maintain the same random seed and loop range so the results are comparable.

To execute this, I’ll issue a Bash command via the tool. I’ll set a generous timeout (900 seconds) to cover the compile warm‑up plus the 20‑step measurement, and I’ll include a short description “Compiled model benchmark, auto dynamic” – even though I’m not using the `dynamic=True` flag, the description just signals that this is the next step after the dynamic failure. The command will import the necessary modules, instantiate the model on CUDA, compile it (static mode), generate dummy input, define the `step` function with autocast, run the warm‑up loops, then time the 20 random steps and print both the warm‑up duration and the per‑step latency along with the derived megatokens‑per‑second metric.

All set – I’ll now run this Bash snippet to see if the static compilation succeeds and to collect the performance numbers.
